The Algerian minnow (Pseudophoxinus callensis) reaches a maximum adult body length of 10.7 cm [Li = 10.7 cm], placing it among the smaller cyprinids endemic to North African freshwater systems. Field surveys conducted throughout its range in Algeria and Tunisia indicate that individuals rarely exceed this asymptotic size, with growth rates slowing considerably after the onset of gonadal maturation. The species typically attains sexual maturity at a total length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a threshold that corresponds to the transition from the juvenile growth phase to reproductive competence. At this length, the wet weight of an individual at puberty averages approximately 1.17 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.17 grams], as estimated from length–weight regressions derived from local population samples. Comparatively, the ultimate wet weight of fully grown adults has been recorded at 12.3 grams [Wwi = 12.3 grams], representing a roughly tenfold increase in body mass from the size at first maturity. These morphological parameters align closely with those of other small-bodied leuciscine cyprinids inhabiting Mediterranean climate zones, where seasonal resource limitation imposes a premium on early maturation and modest terminal size.

Reproductive investment in the Algerian minnow begins with the production of small, demersal eggs, each measuring approximately 1.5 mm in diameter. From this egg dimension, the calculated wet weight at birth for newly emerged yolk-sac larvae is 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], reflecting the modest maternal provisioning typical of species that produce numerous small offspring rather than a few large ones. Following eclosion, the prolarvae remain in a lecithotrophic state for several days, relying entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of first exogenous feeding. The transition to active feeding is a critical bottleneck in the early life history, as larvae must locate suitable zooplankton prey before their energy stores are exhausted. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum daily egg output per female has been estimated at slightly more than one egg per day, which translates to approximately 430 eggs produced over the course of a full year [Ri = approximately 430 eggs produced over the course of a full year]. This moderate reproductive rate is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy, where females distribute their reproductive effort across multiple spawning events rather than investing all energy into a single, large clutch.

Longevity records for this species indicate that individuals can survive for up to ten years [am = up to ten years] when maintained under stable captive conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], though field-based estimates of maximum lifespan are often lower owing to predation pressure and seasonal habitat desiccation. This decadelong potential lifespan is notably extended for a fish of such small body size, suggesting that the Algerian minnow employs a relatively slow pace of life compared to many other cyprinids of equivalent mass. The trade-off between somatic maintenance and reproductive output is reflected in the modest annual reproductive allocation, which allows individuals to persist across multiple breeding seasons. Growth analyses based on otolith increment counts reveal that most of the ultimate body length is achieved within the first two to three years, after which somatic expansion plateaus and energy is increasingly diverted toward gamete production. The capacity for such extended survival is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable hydrological regimes of Mediterranean temporary streams, where years of drought may preclude successful reproduction altogether.

The reproductive phenology of Pseudophoxinus callensis is tightly coupled to seasonal temperature cycles, with spawning activity concentrated during the spring months when water temperatures approach the optimal thermal regime for embryonic development. At 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the period from fertilisation to hatching is relatively brief, facilitated by the rapid cleavage divisions characteristic of teleost embryos developing in warm waters. Field observations indicate that females may spawn multiple clutches within a single breeding season, releasing adhesive eggs that attach to submerged vegetation or gravel substrates. The interval between successive spawning events appears to be influenced by both temperature and food availability, as females require sufficient time to undergo vitellogenesis and accumulate yolk protein precursors in the ovary. After the completion of the reproductive season, adults enter a period of somatic recovery during the hot, dry summer months, when metabolic demands are elevated but foraging opportunities diminish. This seasonal patterning of energy allocation ensures that reproductive effort coincides with the period of highest larval food abundance and lowest risk of habitat desiccation.

Comparative life-history data from congeneric species suggest that the Algerian minnow occupies a conservative position along the fast–slow continuum, prioritising adult survival over high instantaneous fecundity. The ultimate total length of 10.7 cm [Li = 10.7 cm] represents a stable upper boundary that has been documented across multiple populations separated by geographic barriers, indicating strong genetic canalisation of body size. Similarly, the wet weight at puberty of 1.17 grams [Wwp = 1.17 grams] and the adult asymptotic mass of 12.3 grams [Wwi = 12.3 grams] exhibit low coefficients of variation among sampled localities, reinforcing the notion that these parameters are under stabilizing selection.
